title: Vishnu is born as Rama
hookLine: Dasharatha's long wait; God comes down as his son
carry: avatar: god comes down to set things right

cards: Ayodhya. A shining city on a river, with walls and gardens and elephants, and a good king named Dasharatha. His name means ten chariots.
He has wealth, peace, and three queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And no son. Year after year, the kingdom waits for an heir, and the king grows old.
And far above Ayodhya, the gods have a problem of their own.

teach.h: RAVANA: NO GOD CAN KILL HIM.
teach.b: This is the opening of the Ramayana, the story of Rama. Tradition says Valmiki composed it, and calls him the first poet. For the next five weeks, i'll walk you through it, one scene a day.
Here's the trouble above the clouds. A demon king, Ravana, has won a boon: no god, no demon, no spirit can kill him. He never thought to ask about humans; they seemed too small to matter.
So the gods go to Vishnu, the preserver, and Vishnu makes a choice: he will be born as a human, as Dasharatha's son.

teach.h: A FIRE, A GOLDEN BOWL, FOUR SONS.
teach.b: Back on earth, Dasharatha holds a great fire ritual for sons, led by a young sage, Rishyashringa. Out of the flames rises a shining figure carrying a golden bowl of sweet rice pudding, payasa.
Give this to your queens, he says. In time, four sons are born. Kausalya bears Rama.
Kaikeyi bears Bharata. Sumitra bears twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Remember the name Kaikeyi.
Hindus call it avatara, a word that means coming down. Many Hindus believe that when the world tips badly out of balance, God doesn't only fix it from far away.

teach.h: AVATAR: GOD COMES DOWN TO SET THINGS RIGHT.
teach.b: God comes down, and is born as one of us: a baby, in a family, in a house with worried parents. Rama is honored as Vishnu's avatar.

That's why, on Rama's birthday, Rama Navami, many temples and homes place a small image of baby Rama in a cradle and rock it at midday, the hour tradition gives for his birth. The old king asked for an heir.
God came to live in his house.

how: Many Hindus read the Ramayana in their own language, recite it at home or in temples, and watch it performed as Ramlila each autumn; Rama's birthday is celebrated as Rama Navami in spring.

o: a king's vow to give up his throne for an heir
a fire ritual offered for the wish of a son
a naming ceremony held for a newborn prince

games.q: who was born to whom — tap the pairs.

s: the Ramayana begins with a battle
it begins with an old king waiting for a child, and a god choosing to be born.
God comes down and is born as one of us. Rama is honored as Vishnu's avatar.
Ravana's boon protected him from humans too
he never asked about humans. he thought they were too small to matter.

games.q: you're Vishnu. a demon king can't be killed by any god, and the world is tipping out of balance. what do you do?
o: throw a thunderbolt from the sky.
be born as a human child, in a king's house.
wait for the demon king to grow old.
games.why: he chooses to come down: born as Rama, Dasharatha's son. Hindus call this avatara.

practice: Many Hindus repeat Rama's name as a prayer, softly, with the breath. Try it for a couple of minutes: breathe in, and as you breathe out, say Ram, out loud or in your head.
If you'd rather not pray, picture your own ordinary rooms and ask what it would mean if the holy came to live right there, not far away.

wordCard.voice: Putrakameshti, the fire ritual for the wish of a son, after years of Dasharatha's waiting. A golden bowl comes from the flames, four sons are born, and the eldest, Rama, is Vishnu come down.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the sacrifice (ishti) for the desire (kama) of a son (putra).

carryVoice: Your line: avatar, God comes down to set things right. Not only from far away: born into a family, in a house. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 15–16 (Ravana's boon leaves out humans; Vishnu agrees to be born as Dasharatha's son)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 8–18 (Dasharatha's wish; the sacrifice; the payasa; the four births, Rama on the ninth day of Chaitra)
Bhagavad Gita 4.7–8 (God comes whenever dharma declines; background for avatara, not named in the script)
